tRNA. Transfer RNA is a small RNA molecule that delivers amino acids to the ribosome during protein synthesis. Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and possesses an anticodon, a three-base sequence that pairs with complementary mRNA codons. This anticodon-codon matching is the molecular mechanism that translates the genetic code into protein sequences, making tRNA the interpreter between nucleic acids and proteins.

tRNA is a cloverleaf-shaped RNA that folds into an L-shaped three-dimensional structure in the ribosome.

Each tRNA is charged, or loaded, with a specific amino acid by an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase enzyme.

The anticodon, typically located in the anticodon loop, base-pairs with an mRNA codon, ensuring correct amino acid insertion.

tRNA occupies three sites on the ribosome during translation. These are the A site, or aminoacyl, where incoming tRNA enters; the P site, or peptidyl, where the current tRNA resides; and the E site, or exit, where the leaving tRNA departs.

Multiple tRNAs may recognize the same amino acid due to wobble base pairing at the third codon position.

In the ribosome, peptide bonds form between amino acids carried by consecutive tRNAs, extending the growing chain.

Human cells employ roughly 40 to 60 different tRNA species to cover the 61 sense codons and their variations.

The three-prime CCA tail of tRNA is where the amino acid attaches. This end is added post-transcriptionally and is highly conserved.

Mutations in tRNA genes or recognition sites can cause genetic diseases. Some cancers exploit tRNA mischarging for cell survival.

tRNA structure and interactions are among the most highly conserved features across all domains of life, underscoring their evolutionary importance.
